parts:
Hello, 

I am afraid that I come back bothering again...
In a geostatistical model with a Gaussian family, is it possible to get some log-density score ? Something like 
\int log(p(y|\theta, \beta)) p(\beta, \theta | y) d \beta, \theta
y being the observations, and \beta, \theta respectively the Gaussian effects and the high-level parameters of the model. I had a look at control.compute but I found nothing. 

Kind regards and thank you for all the work on INLA
Sébastien

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Log- density score for Gaussian observations
parts:
Hi Sébastien,

Inla can provide leave-one-out log-predictive-density scores directly (log(CPO)), but I think you’re asking about more general predictive scores, e.g. with hold-out data?

There’s a vignette discussing this in the inlabru context at https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html
That discusses the general problem of computing posterior prediction scores as well as gives more details in the case of Poisson count predictions.
For plain inla, the same techniques can be used, by directly calling inla.posterior.sample() and postprocessing the output (thats what the inlabru generate() and predict() functions do).

Finn

Hello,

First, thank Finn for everything ! I will look into it !  

Haavard, as for your remark, in the Gaussian setting, I feel that the formula with the log inside the \int is some Bayesian extension of the Mean Squared Error, R-squared, and so on. 
we get MSE = \sum((y-X\hat\beta - \hat w)^2)
\hat w being the chosen point estimate of the latent field, \hat\beta the point estimate of the regression coefficients for the fixed effects.
If we want to predict a (Gaussian) distribution instead of fixed values, we can do this by weighting by the noise standard deviation \hat s. 
 MSE = \sum(( (y-X\hat\beta - \hat w) / \hat s)^2)
Here for example, if we have a heteroskedastic noise, instead of having a brutish MSE who is happy when the squares are low and angry when the squares are high, we get something that will assess the confidence with which the prediction is done, and punish both errors made confidently and good answers made hesitantly.  
But then again, we have a Bayesian model so we have some incertitude on the parameters. My way to plug that in is to integrate over \beta, w, and s, giving the "log-inside" formula. 
Do you think I am overlooking something there ?

Thanks to you all
Sébastien

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Log- density score for Gaussian observations
parts:
Hi,

I didn’t notice you didn’t have the version Haavard suggested, and instead used the expectation of the conditional score,

Eλ|data[S(Fλ,y)]

This issue is discussed in the vignette; in particular, it mentions the problems with improper scores this appears to result in, see https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html#posterior-expectation-of-conditional-scores
I would strongly encourage you to look up the Gneiting and Raftery JASA paper (mid-2000s) on proper scoring rules.

(Y-mu)^2/s^2 is not a proper score, as it can be reduced to zero by choosing s=infty.
But if you add log(s^2), it becomes a proper score(the Dawid-Sebastiani score, which is the same as the log-score for Gaussian data).

Finn

Le jeudi 14 décembre 2023 à 12:49:55 UTC+1, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
Hi,

I didn’t notice you didn’t have the version Haavard suggested, and instead used the expectation of the conditional score,

Eλ|data[S(Fλ,y)]

This issue is discussed in the vignette; in particular, it mentions the problems with improper scores this appears to result in, see https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/prediction_scores.html#posterior-expectation-of-conditional-scores
I would strongly encourage you to look up the Gneiting and Raftery JASA paper (mid-2000s) on proper scoring rules.

(Y-mu)^2/s^2 is not a proper score, as it can be reduced to zero by choosing s=infty.
But if you add log(s^2), it becomes a proper score(the Dawid-Sebastiani score, which is the same as the log-score for Gaussian data).

Finn

On 14 Dec 2023, at 12:15, Sébastien Coube <sebasti...@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿Hello,

First, thank Finn for everything ! I will look into it !  

Haavard, as for your remark, in the Gaussian setting, I feel that the formula with the log inside the \int is some Bayesian extension of the Mean Squared Error, R-squared, and so on. 
we get MSE = \sum((y-X\hat\beta - \hat w)^2)
\hat w being the chosen point estimate of the latent field, \hat\beta the point estimate of the regression coefficients for the fixed effects.
If we want to predict a (Gaussian) distribution instead of fixed values, we can do this by weighting by the noise standard deviation \hat s. 
 MSE = \sum(( (y-X\hat\beta - \hat w) / \hat s)^2)
Here for example, if we have a heteroskedastic noise, instead of having a brutish MSE who is happy when the squares are low and angry when the squares are high, we get something that will assess the confidence with which the prediction is done, and punish both errors made confidently and good answers made hesitantly.  
But then again, we have a Bayesian model so we have some incertitude on the parameters. My way to plug that in is to integrate over \beta, w, and s, giving the "log-inside" formula. 
Do you think I am overlooking something there ?

Thanks to you all
Sébastien
